planting.note: Plant a container or balled-and-burlapped single-trunk specimen in fall or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; give it room to develop its upright oval crown.

directions: Snowcloud is a single-trunk selection of Allegheny serviceberry chosen for markedly faster growth and a tidier, more upright oval form than typical seedling A. laevis. Bronze-red new foliage unfurls beneath heavy drooping clusters of white flowers in early spring, followed by June berries that ripen from red through purple to near-black and are good for fresh eating or baking if harvested ahead of the birds. Foliage holds up well through summer heat and humidity before turning coppery orange to red in fall. Site it in full sun to light shade and moist, well-drained soil, and use it as a specimen or street tree where a single clean trunk is preferred over a multi-stemmed clump.

planting.note: Plant a container or balled-and-burlapped tree in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; its strong central leader needs little corrective pruning to stay tree-form.

directions: Introduced by Lake County Nursery, Tradition is valued because it naturally grows a single dominant trunk rather than the multi-stemmed clump typical of shadblow serviceberry, making it a practical choice for street tree plantings, standards, and formal specimen use. Late-April clouds of white flowers give way to heavy crops of blue-black June berries that draw songbirds and can be picked for jams and baking if reached first. Fall color runs orange to red, and the tree tolerates a range of soils as long as drainage is reasonable. Plant in full sun to light shade and water regularly through the first two seasons to establish its central leader form.

planting.note: Set out dormant or container nursery stock in early spring in full sun; plant a blue-fruited saskatoon cultivar nearby since Altaglow needs a pollinizer to set its ivory-white fruit.

directions: Selected from wild stock in Alberta and released through the Brooks Horticultural Research Station, Altaglow is an erect, narrow, multi-stemmed saskatoon grown chiefly as a hardy prairie ornamental rather than a commercial fruit crop. Its most distinctive feature is fruit that ripens ivory to pale yellow-white instead of the usual blue-black, turning brown if left to dry on the shrub; because it is self-sterile, plant it alongside a standard blue-fruited saskatoon to ensure pollination and any fruit set at all. Clusters of white spring flowers precede foliage that turns gold, red, and deep purple in a long-lasting fall display, and the columnar habit suits narrow screens, windbreak rows, or foundation plantings on the northern prairies. It tolerates severe cold, wind, and a wide range of soils once established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and allow room for the clump to widen as it suckers.

directions: Prince William is a compact, bushy, suckering selection of shadblow serviceberry that stays well under the size of the straight species, making it a better fit for foundation plantings and smaller shade gardens. It is self-fertile and produces unusually heavy crops of sweet, blue, blueberry-like fruit that ripen in early summer and are excellent fresh, baked, or left for birds. Bronze-toned new growth matures to green and finishes the season in a mix of yellow, orange, red, and purple. Give it moist, well-drained soil and full sun to light shade for the best flowering and fruit set, and thin out excess suckers periodically if a tighter clump is desired.

planting.note: Plant a container or balled-and-burlapped specimen in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; it can be trained as a single trunk or left as a dense multi-stemmed form.

directions: Patented from a plant found at the University of Wisconsin Arboretum, Prince Charles is a densely branched serviceberry selection notable for opening its full flush of white flowers before the leaves unfold, giving a cleaner, more concentrated bloom display than typical seedling serviceberries. Bronze-purple emerging foliage matures to green through summer and shifts to yellow, orange, and red in fall, while the sweet purple-black June berries are quickly stripped by birds if not netted or picked early. It can be grown as a large multi-stemmed shrub or limbed up into a small single- or multi-trunk tree, and performs best in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade. It combines well with other spring-flowering natives in a woodland-edge or mixed border planting.
